1.meaning: May it perish / be ruined / come to nothing. A curse-prayer asking that the two hands of Abu Lahab — and through them the whole person and all his works — be destroyed and rendered utterly fruitless. It carries the sense of loss, failure, and ruin all at once. The verb is feminine singular because its subject is the pair of hands, which Arabic treats as a single feminine unit; natural English renders this 'may the hands perish.'

parts.en: to perish, be ruined, come to nothing

1.grammar: A past-tense verb (form I) used as a curse/invocation: 'may it perish!' The ending -at (ـَتْ) marks the subject as third-person feminine singular. It is feminine singular — not plural — because the grammatical subject is yadā ('the two hands'); a dual subject takes feminine-singular verb agreement in Arabic, so the verb does not carry a dual or plural marker. Though past in form, the meaning here is an invocation against Abu Lahab, not a report of something already done.
1.root: ت-ب-ب (t-b-b) — to perish, be ruined, suffer loss

2.meaning: The two hands. Literally a dual ('a pair of hands'), but here the hands stand for the whole person and all his deeds and efforts — what someone 'does' is done with the hands, so cursing the hands curses the man and everything he strives for.
2.grammar: This is the dual form of yad ('hand'), so it means exactly 'two hands,' not one or many. It is the subject of the verb 'perish.' The dual normally ends in -āni, but because it is joined ('in construct') to the next word 'Abu (Lahab)' — 'the two hands OF Abu Lahab' — the final -ni drops, leaving just yadā.

3.meaning: Of Abu (literally 'father of'). 'Abu Lahab' is a nickname meaning 'Father of Flame,' given for his glowing, ruddy face; the Qur'an uses the nickname rather than his real name ('Abd al-'Uzza), and the 'flame' in it grimly foreshadows the Fire mentioned later.
3.grammar: This is one of a small set of 'five nouns' that show their case with a long vowel. Here the -ī ending is the genitive (possessive) form, signalling two links at once: 'the hands OF Abu…' (it is possessed by 'hands') and 'Abu OF Lahab' (it owns the next word). So abī = 'father of,' set up to attach to 'Lahab.'

4.meaning: Lahab — literally 'flame' or 'blaze.' As part of the name 'Abu Lahab' ('Father of Flame') it functions as a proper name, but the underlying meaning 'flame' is deliberately chosen and echoes the 'flaming Fire' he is warned of in the next verses.
4.grammar: The final -in (written with the double-vowel mark called tanwīn) does two things: the -i part is genitive because this word is possessed by 'Abu' ('father OF Lahab'), and the -n part marks it as indefinite (no 'the'). Together they give the reading 'Father of Flame.'

5.meaning: And he himself has perished / is ruined. Where the first verb was a prayer ('may it perish'), this closing statement declares it accomplished as a certain fact: he himself is utterly ruined. The shift from invocation to flat statement makes the doom sound sealed.
5.grammar: 'wa' (وَ) means 'and.' 'tabba' is the same form I past-tense verb as in word 1, but here it is third-person masculine singular, so the subject is Abu Lahab himself rather than 'the hands.' Masculine singular is shown by the absence of any subject suffix — there is no ending added at all, in contrast to word 1's feminine -at (ـَتْ). The final -a is simply the short vowel (fatḥa) sitting on the last root letter (the doubled ب); it is part of the verb stem, not a person-marker. Unlike word 1's curse, this reads as a statement of fact: 'and he has perished.'
5.root: ت-ب-ب (t-b-b) — to perish, be ruined, suffer loss

1.meaning: A negating particle meaning "not" / "did not." Here it introduces a flat denial about the past: nothing whatsoever was of any use to him. In context it carries the force of "It availed him nothing."
1.grammar: A standalone negative particle, here negating the past-tense verb that follows. It has no case ending of its own; it simply turns 'availed' into 'did NOT avail.' The lengthening on the alif is a recitation feature, not a grammatical ending.

2.meaning: To avail, to be of use, to ward off need or harm. The sense is that his wealth could not enrich him, protect him, or save him from punishment — it could not make him independent of Allah's judgement.
2.grammar: A past-tense verb, 3rd-person masculine singular ('it availed'). It is Form IV (formed with a prefixed hamza, اَ-, on the root), which makes the verb causative/transitive: 'to make someone free of need,' i.e. 'to benefit/avail.' The root is defective (final-weak), so the past ending surfaces as -ā written with alif maqṣūra (ٰى); the doer ('his wealth') comes later in the sentence.
2.root: غ-ن-ي (gh-n-y) — to be free of need, richness, sufficiency

3.meaning: A two-part word meaning "from him" / "on his behalf," i.e. "for him." It marks the person for whose benefit (in fact, to no benefit) the availing was directed.
3.grammar: A preposition ('ʿan') with an attached pronoun ('-hu' = him). The pronoun is in the object form required after a preposition. Together they tell us the wealth did not avail 'for/from him' — pinning the benefit that never came to Abu Lahab specifically.

4.meaning: His wealth, his property and riches — the money and possessions he relied on and boasted of. This is the grammatical subject: the thing that failed to help him.
4.grammar: A noun ('māl' = wealth) plus the attached possessive pronoun '-hu' (his). The -u ending on 'mālu' is the nominative case, marking this as the doer/subject of the verb 'availed' — it is 'his wealth' that did the (non-)availing.

5.meaning: "And what..." — a connector joining a second subject to the first. It links 'his wealth' with the further thing that failed him, introducing 'whatever he earned/acquired.'
5.grammar: Two particles: 'wa' (and) joining this to 'his wealth,' and 'mā' here used not as a negative but as a relative pronoun meaning 'what / that which.' So the second subject of 'availed' is 'and that which he earned.' These particles take no case ending.

6.meaning: What he earned, gained, or acquired — the fruits of his striving. Classical commentators note this also covers his children, since in Arabic one's offspring are counted among one's 'earnings.' Neither his gains nor his sons could rescue him.
6.grammar: A past-tense verb, 3rd-person masculine singular: 'he earned.' The final -a is the standard past-tense ending for 'he (did).' It sits inside the relative clause begun by 'mā,' giving 'that which he earned.' Together with 'his wealth,' it forms the compound subject of 'availed him nothing.'

1.meaning: He will soon roast in, be burned by, and scorched by the Fire. The verb describes being seared and consumed by fire, suffering its full heat. The attached future marker stresses that this is a certain, impending outcome awaiting him.
1.grammar: A present/future verb made future by the prefix sa- ('will, shall soon'). The ya- prefix marks a single male subject: 'he'. The verb ends in a long -ā (written with alif maqṣūra) because its final root letter is weak; it carries the indicative meaning of a real, certain event. Sense: 'he will surely be burned/roasted.'
1.root: ص-ل-ي (ṣ-l-y) — to roast, burn, be scorched by fire

2.meaning: A fire — here the Fire of punishment in the Hereafter. It is left grammatically indefinite, which in this context magnifies it: 'a fire' of a terrible, indescribable kind.
2.grammar: A noun in the accusative case, shown by the final -an (tanwīn fatḥa). The accusative marks it as the object/goal of the verb — what he will be burned in. The -an ending also signals that the noun is indefinite: 'a fire.'
2.root: ن-و-ر (n-w-r) — the sense of burning/blazing fire; the noun نَار ('fire') belongs to this root (distinct from نُور, 'light,' from the same root)

3.meaning: Possessor of / having / full of. This word means 'one that possesses' a quality; here it links the Fire to its defining feature, describing it as a fire that owns and is characterized by flame.
3.grammar: The feminine form of dhū ('possessor of'). It is in the accusative case, shown by the final -a, because it describes the accusative noun 'fire' (nār is feminine, so the feminine dhāt agrees with it). It is grammatically bound to the word after it, meaning 'having ___ / possessor of ___.'
3.root: — (a possessive word; no verbal triliteral root)

4.meaning: Flame — the leaping, blazing tongues of fire. Describing the Fire as 'possessor of flame' paints it as fiercely blazing. The word also echoes the name Abu Lahab ('father of flame'), tying his fate to the very thing his nickname evoked.
4.grammar: A noun in the genitive case, shown by the final -in (tanwīn kasra). It is genitive because it follows dhāta ('possessor of'), forming a possessive link (iḍāfa): 'possessor OF flame' = 'full of flame.' The -in ending also marks it as indefinite.
4.root: ل-ه-ب (l-h-b) — to blaze, flame up; flame

1.meaning: "And his wife" — i.e. the wife of Abu Lahab, Umm Jamil. The opening "and" (waw) connects this verse to the previous ones: she shares in the punishment alongside her husband. The word for "wife" here is the ordinary word for "woman," used in the sense of a man's spouse, with "his" pointing back to Abu Lahab.
1.grammar: Starts with the connecting word "and" (wa-), joining this verse to what precedes. The noun "imraʾah" (woman/wife) here appears in its bound (construct) form imraʾatu-: because the possessive suffix is attached, the feminine ـة is pronounced as a full -t- (giving -atu-), not silenced as it would be in the standalone citation form. The attached ـهٗ (-hu) means "his," referring to Abu Lahab. The case ending is -u (nominative) because this noun is the mubtadaʾ (subject/topic) of its own nominal sentence in this verse; its predicate is the following description (she is "the carrier of firewood"), or an implied clause that she too will enter the Fire.
1.root: م-ر-ء (m-r-ʾ) — person / human being; feminine form: woman, wife

2.meaning: "The carrier (of)" — a feminine intensive form describing someone who habitually and abundantly carries a load. The doubled, heavy pattern conveys that she does this constantly and zealously: she is the wood-hauler. It also carries a figurative sense in tafsir — one who spreads slander, "carrying tales" — and a literal sense of one who carried thorns to harm the Prophet (peace be upon him), and who will carry firewood to feed the Fire in the Hereafter.
2.grammar: This is an intensive doer-form (the faʿʿaal pattern, with the middle letter doubled) made feminine by the ـة ending — "one who carries a great deal." The doubling stresses repetition and intensity. Its final ending is -a (accusative): it is grammatically "in the accusative" either as a description in apposition giving her a disparaging title, or read as a noun of dispraise ("the wood-carrier that she is!"), which is why it shows -a rather than the -u you might expect for a simple subject.
2.root: ح-م-ل (ḥ-m-l) — to carry, bear, haul a load

3.meaning: "Of the firewood" — the dry wood/kindling that she carries. Literally the fuel gathered for burning. Commentators explain it both literally (firewood, or the thorns she strewed in the Prophet's path) and figuratively (the "fuel" of slander she carried between people), and as the wood she will bear in Hell.
3.grammar: Begins with the definite article al- ("the"). The stem "ḥaṭab" (firewood) carries the ending -i (genitive): the -i marks it as the thing possessed by "carrier," giving the meaning "carrier OF the firewood" — the genitive link is exactly what English shows with "of."
3.root: ح-ط-ب (ḥ-ṭ-b) — firewood, to gather wood for fuel

1.meaning: A locational particle meaning "in," "inside," or "upon." Here it sets the scene of the punishment by placing what follows (a rope) physically on a specific spot — her neck. It governs the word after it, putting it into the genitive case.
1.grammar: An indeclinable preposition (a fixed little word that never changes its form). Its job is to point to a location: "in/on her neck." Whatever noun comes after it must take the genitive ending — which is exactly why the next word reads jīdi-hā (with an -i) rather than jīdu-hā.

2.meaning: Her neck — specifically the neck or throat region where a necklace or collar would sit. The reference is to the wife of Abu Lahab, and the image is grimly ironic: the place she once adorned with jewellery now bears a rope of torment.
2.grammar: A noun followed by an attached possessive pronoun. The -i ending on jīdi is genitive, caused by the preposition fī before it ("in her neck"). The suffix -hā means "her," referring to a single female; because this pronoun is possessing the noun, the two together form an "of" relationship — literally "the neck of her."

3.meaning: A rope or cord — a length of twisted strands used for binding or hanging. Left deliberately indefinite ("a rope"), which in Arabic can suggest something dreadful and beyond description. It is the subject of the sentence: a rope is/will be on her neck.
3.grammar: A singular noun carrying the ending -un, a form of tanwīn (nunation) written above the final letter as two small ḍamma strokes (tiny curly hooks), not as two dots. That doubled-vowel ending marks the word as indefinite — "a rope," not "the rope." The -u within it is the nominative case, which signals that this word is the subject of the clause (the thing being described as being on her neck). In English the linking verb "is/will be" is supplied, since Arabic leaves it unspoken here.

4.meaning: A particle meaning "of," "from," or "made out of." Here it expresses material or origin — the rope is made from / consists of the substance named next. It links the rope to what it is fashioned out of.
4.grammar: An indeclinable preposition (a fixed word that does not change form). It governs the following noun and forces it into the genitive case — which is why the next word ends in -in. In this context it conveys "made of / consisting of," describing the rope's material.

5.meaning: Masad — palm-fibre: a coarse rope twisted from the fibres of the date palm. Classical commentators also explain it can mean a tightly twisted cord, or, in the Fire, a chain of iron. The word is left indefinite to heighten its harshness. There is deliberate sound-play with "lahab" (flame) earlier in the surah.
5.grammar: A singular noun with the ending -in, a form of tanwīn (nunation) written beneath the final letter as two small kasra strokes. The -i part is the genitive case, required because the preposition min comes before it ("of palm-fibre"). The tanwīn (the doubled vowel) marks it as indefinite — "some palm-fibre," an unspecified, dreadful material. Being the last word, it carries the verse's rhyme.
5.root: م-س-د (m-s-d) — to twist / tightly wind (a fibre rope)
